cards.statement: Monitoring of abnormal activities and behaviour is best associated with the detection component of a fraud control framework.
cards.explanation: Detective controls such as supervision, monitoring and alerts identify abnormal behaviour after it occurs so that the impact of fraud is limited.
cards.originalText: Detection.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
cards.loText: Describe elements of a control framework to manage financial fraud risk and money laundering risk.
cards.reading: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
cards.statement: Monitoring of abnormal activities and behaviour is best associated with the prevention component of a fraud control framework.
cards.explanation: Prevention consists of controls such as limiting access rights and segregating duties that stop fraud occurring. Monitoring for abnormal behaviour is detection.
cards.originalText: Prevention.
cards.correction: Monitoring of abnormal activities and behaviour is best associated with the detection component of a fraud control framework.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.loText: Calculate and interpret the RAROC for a project, loan, or loan portfolio and use RAROC to compare business unit performance.
cards.reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.statement: In the capital-budgeting formula for RAROC, expected losses are deducted from expected revenues in the numerator, along with costs and taxes.
cards.explanation: Capital-budgeting RAROC is (expected revenues - costs - expected losses - taxes + return on risk capital +/- transfers) divided by economic capital.
cards.originalText: Expected losses

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.loText: Calculate and interpret the RAROC for a project, loan, or loan portfolio and use RAROC to compare business unit performance.
cards.reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.statement: The Sharpe ratio is an input to the calculation of RAROC.
cards.explanation: The Sharpe ratio is a comparable risk-return measure, not a RAROC input. RAROC uses revenues, costs, expected losses, taxes, return on risk capital, transfers and economic capital.
cards.originalText: Sharpe ratio

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.loText: Calculate and interpret the RAROC for a project, loan, or loan portfolio and use RAROC to compare business unit performance.
cards.reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.statement: Net present value is an input to the calculation of RAROC.
cards.explanation: NPV is a related but separate performance measure, not a RAROC input. RAROC uses revenues, costs, expected losses, taxes, return on risk capital, transfers and economic capital.
cards.originalText: Net present value

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.loText: Calculate the adjusted RAROC for a project to determine its viability.
cards.reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.statement: Under the adjusted RAROC criterion, a project should be rejected when its adjusted RAROC is lower than the market expected excess return.
cards.explanation: Once RAROC is adjusted for systematic risk, the benchmark is the risk-free rate, not the market excess return. A project is accepted if ARAROC exceeds the risk-free rate.
cards.originalText: Reject the project because the ARAROC is lower than the market expected excess return.
cards.correction: Under the adjusted RAROC criterion, a project should be rejected when its adjusted RAROC is lower than the risk-free rate.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.loText: Calculate the adjusted RAROC for a project to determine its viability.
cards.reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.statement: Under the adjusted RAROC criterion, a project should be rejected when its adjusted RAROC is lower than the risk-free rate.
cards.explanation: Adjusted RAROC equals RAROC minus beta times the market excess return, and it must exceed the risk-free rate for the project to be accepted.
cards.originalText: Reject the project because the adjusted RAROC is lower than the risk‑free rate.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.loText: Calculate the adjusted RAROC for a project to determine its viability.
cards.reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.statement: Adjusted RAROC deducts a charge for a project's systematic risk, so the same hurdle rate, the risk-free rate, applies across all projects and business lines.
cards.explanation: ARAROC = RAROC - beta x (market return - risk-free rate) strips out the return that merely compensates for non-diversifiable risk, so every project is judged against the risk-free rate.
cards.originalText: ARAROC deducts a charge for the project’s systematic risk, so that the same hurdle rate (the risk‑free rate) applies across all projects and business lines

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.loText: Calculate the adjusted RAROC for a project to determine its viability.
cards.reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.statement: Adjusted RAROC replaces economic capital in the denominator with regulatory capital.
cards.explanation: The adjustment changes the numerator by deducting the beta-based systematic-risk charge. It does not change the capital definition, and regulatory capital is not substituted.
cards.originalText: ARAROC replaces economic capital in the denominator with regulatory capital

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe measures introduced in the 1995 and 1996 amendments, including guidelines for netting of credit exposures and methods for calculating market risk capital for assets in the trading book.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The standardized measurement method was one of the two methods allowed by the 1996 Amendment to Basel I for measuring market risk.
cards.explanation: The 1996 Amendment allowed market risk capital to be calculated with either the standardized measurement method or the internal model-based approach (bank VaR model).
cards.originalText: Standardized measurement method

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe measures introduced in the 1995 and 1996 amendments, including guidelines for netting of credit exposures and methods for calculating market risk capital for assets in the trading book.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The current exposure method was one of the two methods allowed by the 1996 Amendment to Basel I for measuring market risk.
cards.explanation: The current exposure method estimates the credit equivalent amount of derivatives for credit risk. The market risk methods were the standardized measurement method and the internal model-based approach.
cards.originalText: Current exposure method
cards.correction: The standardized measurement method was one of the two methods allowed by the 1996 Amendment to Basel I for measuring market risk.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe measures introduced in the 1995 and 1996 amendments, including guidelines for netting of credit exposures and methods for calculating market risk capital for assets in the trading book.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The foundation internal ratings-based approach was one of the two methods allowed by the 1996 Amendment to Basel I for measuring market risk.
cards.explanation: Foundation IRB is a Basel II credit risk approach and did not exist in 1996. The market risk methods were the standardized measurement method and the internal model-based approach.
cards.originalText: Foundation internal ratings‑based approach
cards.correction: The standardized measurement method was one of the two methods allowed by the 1996 Amendment to Basel I for measuring market risk.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe measures introduced in the 1995 and 1996 amendments, including guidelines for netting of credit exposures and methods for calculating market risk capital for assets in the trading book.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under the 1996 Amendment, banks meeting several criteria, including daily backtesting, could use their own internal value at risk model to determine capital requirements for market risk.
cards.explanation: Allowing qualifying banks to use internal VaR models, subject to a multiplier and backtesting, was the key innovation of the 1996 Amendment.
cards.originalText: Conditional on meeting several criteria, including daily backtesting, banks could now employ their own internal value at risk (VaR) model to determine capital requirements for market risk

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe measures introduced in the 1995 and 1996 amendments, including guidelines for netting of credit exposures and methods for calculating market risk capital for assets in the trading book.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The 1996 Amendment introduced the third pillar of the Basel framework.
cards.explanation: The three pillars, including Pillar 3 market discipline, were introduced with Basel II in 2004, not with the 1996 Amendment.
cards.originalText: It introduced the third pillar, which was praised for giving supervisors a consistent rule‑enforcing playbook
cards.correction: Basel II introduced the third pillar of the Basel framework.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe measures introduced in the 1995 and 1996 amendments, including guidelines for netting of credit exposures and methods for calculating market risk capital for assets in the trading book.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The 1996 Amendment removed Tier 2 capital so that only Tier 1 capital remained.
cards.explanation: The Amendment created Tier 3 capital for market risk and kept Tier 2. The emphasis on common equity within Tier 1 is a Basel III development.
cards.originalText: It removed Tier 2 capital so that only Tier 1 capital remained, with Tier 1 split into common equity and non‑common equity

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe measures introduced in the 1995 and 1996 amendments, including guidelines for netting of credit exposures and methods for calculating market risk capital for assets in the trading book.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The 1996 Amendment eliminated the standardized measurement method for market risk and abolished the distinction between the banking book and the trading book.
cards.explanation: The Amendment introduced the standardized measurement method alongside the internal model-based approach, and it relied on the distinction between the trading book and the banking book.
cards.originalText: The 1996 Amendment eliminated the standardized measurement method for the calculation of market risk and abolished the distinction between the banking and trading books due to widespread regulatory arbitrage between the two
cards.correction: The 1996 Amendment introduced the standardized measurement method for market risk and relied on the distinction between the banking book and the trading book.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe measures introduced in the 1995 and 1996 amendments, including guidelines for netting of credit exposures and methods for calculating market risk capital for assets in the trading book.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The trading book consists of instruments that are actively traded and marked to market daily, whereas the banking book consists primarily of loans held to maturity that are not marked to market daily.
cards.explanation: Trading book positions are held for trading and marked to market. Banking book assets, mainly loans held to maturity, are not.
cards.originalText: The trading book consists of instruments that are actively traded and marked to market daily; the banking book consists primarily of loans that are held to maturity and not marked to market daily

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe measures introduced in the 1995 and 1996 amendments, including guidelines for netting of credit exposures and methods for calculating market risk capital for assets in the trading book.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The 1996 Amendment introduced a capital charge for the market risk associated with all items in the trading book.
cards.explanation: The Amendment added a market risk capital charge on trading book items, calculated by the standardized measurement method or the internal model-based approach.
cards.originalText: The 1996 Amendment introduced a capital charge for the market risk associated with all items in the trading book

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe measures introduced in the 1995 and 1996 amendments, including guidelines for netting of credit exposures and methods for calculating market risk capital for assets in the trading book.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: A bank that uses the historical simulation approach to calculate its value at risk under the internal model-based approach does not need to backtest, because historical simulation is effectively already a backtest.
cards.explanation: Backtesting is mandatory for every internal VaR model, whatever method computes the VaR. The number of backtest exceptions drives the multiplier applied to VaR.
cards.originalText: If a bank elects to use the historical simulation (HS) approach to calculating its value‑at‑risk (VaR), then a backtest is not required because an HS is effectively already a backtest

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe measures introduced in the 1995 and 1996 amendments, including guidelines for netting of credit exposures and methods for calculating market risk capital for assets in the trading book.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: In the internal model-based approach of the 1996 Amendment, the value at risk measure is calculated with a 10-day time horizon and a 99.0% confidence level.
cards.explanation: Regulatory market risk VaR uses a 10-day horizon and 99% confidence, while backtesting uses the one-day 99% VaR.
cards.originalText: In the internal model‑based approach (IMA), the value‑at‑risk (VaR) measure used is calculated with a 10‑day time horizon and a 99.0% confidence level

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe measures introduced in the 1995 and 1996 amendments, including guidelines for netting of credit exposures and methods for calculating market risk capital for assets in the trading book.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under the standardized approach, capital is assigned separately to debt securities, equity securities, foreign exchange risk, commodities risk and options, and no account is taken of correlations between different types of instruments.
cards.explanation: The standardized method charges each category separately and recognises no cross-category correlation or diversification.
cards.originalText: The standardized approach assigns capital separately to each of debt securities, equity securities, foreign exchange risk, commodities risk, and options; but no account is taken for correlations between different types of instruments

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe measures introduced in the 1995 and 1996 amendments, including guidelines for netting of credit exposures and methods for calculating market risk capital for assets in the trading book.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Most large banks preferred the internal model-based approach because it better reflected the benefits of diversification and led to lower capital requirements.
cards.explanation: Internal models recognise diversification, so their capital is generally lower than under the standardized method, which is why banks with material trading books preferred them.
cards.originalText: Most large banks preferred to use the internal model‑based approach because it better reflected the benefits of diversification and led to lower capital requirements

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe measures introduced in the 1995 and 1996 amendments, including guidelines for netting of credit exposures and methods for calculating market risk capital for assets in the trading book.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under the 1996 Amendment, a specific risk capital charge is required for fixed income and equity positions under the standardized method and for positions under the internal model-based approach.
cards.explanation: A VaR model captures only general market movements, so company-specific (issuer-specific) risk needs its own charge under every approach.
cards.originalText: Fixed income and equity positions under the standardized method, and positions under the internal model‑based approach

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe measures introduced in the 1995 and 1996 amendments, including guidelines for netting of credit exposures and methods for calculating market risk capital for assets in the trading book.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under the 1996 Amendment, a specific risk capital charge is required only for positions measured under the internal model-based approach.
cards.explanation: Banks using the standardized method also hold specific risk capital for fixed income and equity positions, so a charge is required under every approach.
cards.originalText: Only positions measured under the internal model‑based approach

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Compare the standardized internal ratings-based (IRB) approach, the foundation IRB approach, and the advanced IRB approach for the calculation of credit risk capital under Basel II.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: When Basel II was implemented in the United States, large internationally active banks were required to use IRB approaches, because the US chose not to implement the Basel II standardized approach.
cards.explanation: US implementation required IRB for internationally active banks and left other banks on an updated version of Basel I rules.
cards.originalText: It was required to use IRB approaches, because the US chose not to implement the Basel II standardized approach.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Compare the standardized internal ratings-based (IRB) approach, the foundation IRB approach, and the advanced IRB approach for the calculation of credit risk capital under Basel II.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: When Basel II was implemented in the United States, large internationally active banks could freely choose among the standardized, foundation IRB and advanced IRB approaches.
cards.explanation: The US did not implement the standardized approach and required internationally active banks to use IRB approaches.
cards.originalText: It could freely choose among the standardized, foundation IRB and advanced IRB approaches.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Compare the standardized internal ratings-based (IRB) approach, the foundation IRB approach, and the advanced IRB approach for the calculation of credit risk capital under Basel II.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The Basel II standardized approach is designed for banks with less sophisticated risk management, and its risk weights depend on asset class and external credit ratings.
cards.explanation: Under the standardized approach the regulator sets the risk weights by asset class and external rating, so no internal models are needed.
cards.originalText: Standardized approach; risk weights depend on asset class and external credit ratings.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Compare the standardized internal ratings-based (IRB) approach, the foundation IRB approach, and the advanced IRB approach for the calculation of credit risk capital under Basel II.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under the Basel II standardized approach, risk weights depend on the bank's own estimates of PD, LGD and EAD.
cards.explanation: Own estimates of PD, LGD and EAD are features of the IRB approaches. Standardized risk weights are set by the regulator and depend on asset class and external ratings.
cards.originalText: Standardized approach; risk weights depend on the bank’s own estimates of PD, LGD and EAD.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Compare the standardized internal ratings-based (IRB) approach, the foundation IRB approach, and the advanced IRB approach for the calculation of credit risk capital under Basel II.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under the Basel II foundation IRB approach, the bank estimates PD, while LGD, EAD and maturity are set by supervisors.
cards.explanation: Foundation IRB gives banks only the PD estimate. LGD (45% senior, 75% subordinated), EAD and maturity (usually 2.5) are supervisory values.
cards.originalText: The bank estimates PD, while LGD, EAD and maturity are set by supervisors.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Compare the standardized internal ratings-based (IRB) approach, the foundation IRB approach, and the advanced IRB approach for the calculation of credit risk capital under Basel II.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under the Basel II foundation IRB approach, supervisors set PD, while the bank estimates LGD and EAD.
cards.explanation: The split is the other way round: the bank estimates PD, while LGD, EAD and maturity are supervisory values.
cards.originalText: Supervisors set PD, while the bank estimates LGD and EAD.
cards.correction: Under the Basel II foundation IRB approach, the bank estimates PD, while supervisors set LGD and EAD.

changes.from: supervisors set PD, while the bank estimates LGD and EAD
changes.to: the bank estimates PD, while supervisors set LGD and EAD

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Compare the standardized internal ratings-based (IRB) approach, the foundation IRB approach, and the advanced IRB approach for the calculation of credit risk capital under Basel II.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under the Basel II advanced IRB approach, the bank itself estimates PD, LGD, EAD and maturity.
cards.explanation: Advanced IRB lets the bank supply all four inputs, subject to supervisory approval, giving the most risk-sensitive credit capital measure.
cards.originalText: PD, LGD, EAD and maturity.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Compare the standardized internal ratings-based (IRB) approach, the foundation IRB approach, and the advanced IRB approach for the calculation of credit risk capital under Basel II.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under the Basel II advanced IRB approach, the bank estimates only LGD, EAD and maturity, while PD is set by supervisors.
cards.explanation: PD is estimated by the bank in both IRB variants, and supervisors never set it. Under advanced IRB the bank also estimates LGD, EAD and maturity.
cards.originalText: LGD, EAD and maturity only; PD is set by supervisors.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Compare the standardized internal ratings-based (IRB) approach, the foundation IRB approach, and the advanced IRB approach for the calculation of credit risk capital under Basel II.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: A bank using the Basel II standardized approach for credit risk assigns to its assets predefined risk weights set by the regulatory authorities.
cards.explanation: The bank classifies its exposures, applies the prescribed risk weights to obtain risk-weighted assets, and holds capital of 8% of RWA, with no internal models.
cards.originalText: Assign predefined risk weights to its assets as set by regulatory authorities.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Compare the standardized internal ratings-based (IRB) approach, the foundation IRB approach, and the advanced IRB approach for the calculation of credit risk capital under Basel II.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: A bank using the Basel II standardized approach for credit risk must calculate the probability of default for each type of asset.
cards.explanation: Own PD estimates are an IRB input. The standardized approach uses regulator-set risk weights based on asset class and external ratings.
cards.originalText: Calculate the probability of default (PD) for each type of asset.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Compare the standardized internal ratings-based (IRB) approach, the foundation IRB approach, and the advanced IRB approach for the calculation of credit risk capital under Basel II.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under the Basel II IRB approach for corporate exposures, capital requirements increase with longer loan maturities, and the maturity adjustment is larger for low-PD borrowers.
cards.explanation: Longer exposures stay on the books longer and have more time to deteriorate. The maturity adjustment depends on PD through b, which falls as PD rises, so low-PD borrowers have the larger adjustment.
cards.originalText: Capital requirements increase with longer loan maturities, and the maturity adjustment is larger for low‑PD borrowers.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Compare the standardized internal ratings-based (IRB) approach, the foundation IRB approach, and the advanced IRB approach for the calculation of credit risk capital under Basel II.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under the Basel II IRB approach for corporate exposures, maturity adjustments are unrelated to PD and depend solely on the loan term.
cards.explanation: The maturity adjustment depends on PD (through the parameter b) as well as on maturity M.
cards.originalText: Maturity adjustments are unrelated to PD and depend solely on the loan term.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Compare the standardized internal ratings-based (IRB) approach, the foundation IRB approach, and the advanced IRB approach for the calculation of credit risk capital under Basel II.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under the Basel II standardized approach, unrated corporate credits receive a lower risk weight than credits rated B+ or lower, which may incentivize banks to lend to unrated companies with poor credit quality.
cards.explanation: Unrated corporates get a 100% risk weight while those rated below BB- get 150%, so the standardized approach can reward lending to weak but unrated borrowers.
cards.originalText: The SA gives lower risk weights to unrated credits than to credits rated B+ or lower, which may incentivize Resource Bank to lend to unrated companies with poor credit quality.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Compare the standardized internal ratings-based (IRB) approach, the foundation IRB approach, and the advanced IRB approach for the calculation of credit risk capital under Basel II.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The advanced IRB approach does not adjust for maturity, which means it could undercapitalise long-dated exposures.
cards.explanation: The IRB formula includes an explicit maturity adjustment that raises capital for exposures longer than one year, so long-dated exposures are not ignored.
cards.originalText: The A‑IRB approach does not adjust for maturity, which means that A‑IRB could undercapitalize the long‑dated exposures at Global Bank.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Compare the standardized internal ratings-based (IRB) approach, the foundation IRB approach, and the advanced IRB approach for the calculation of credit risk capital under Basel II.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The Advanced Measurement Approach is an approach for calculating credit risk capital under Basel II.
cards.explanation: The Advanced Measurement Approach is an operational risk capital method. The Basel II credit risk approaches are the standardized, foundation IRB and advanced IRB approaches.
cards.originalText: Advanced Measurement Approach
cards.correction: The Advanced Measurement Approach is an approach for calculating operational risk capital under Basel II.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Compare the standardized internal ratings-based (IRB) approach, the foundation IRB approach, and the advanced IRB approach for the calculation of credit risk capital under Basel II.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The foundation IRB approach is an approach for calculating credit risk capital under Basel II.
cards.explanation: Basel II offers three credit risk approaches: standardized, foundation IRB and advanced IRB.
cards.originalText: Foundation IRB Approach

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Compare the standardized internal ratings-based (IRB) approach, the foundation IRB approach, and the advanced IRB approach for the calculation of credit risk capital under Basel II.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Basel II offers an advanced version of the standardized approach as one of its approaches for calculating credit risk capital.
cards.explanation: The standardized approach has a single version based on external ratings. Only the IRB approach splits into foundation and advanced versions.
cards.originalText: Standardized approach ‑ Advanced

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Compare the standardized internal ratings-based (IRB) approach, the foundation IRB approach, and the advanced IRB approach for the calculation of credit risk capital under Basel II.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: A bank using the Basel II foundation IRB approach must estimate the probability of default for each type of credit exposure.
cards.explanation: Under foundation IRB the bank supplies only its own PD estimates, while LGD and EAD are prescribed by the regulator.
cards.originalText: Estimating the Probability of Default (PD) for each type of credit exposure

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Compare the standardized internal ratings-based (IRB) approach, the foundation IRB approach, and the advanced IRB approach for the calculation of credit risk capital under Basel II.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: A bank using the Basel II foundation IRB approach must seek external credit ratings for all its credit exposures.
cards.explanation: Reliance on external ratings characterises the standardized approach. Foundation IRB uses the bank's own internal PD estimates.
cards.originalText: Seeking external credit ratings for all its credit exposures

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Compare the standardized internal ratings-based (IRB) approach, the foundation IRB approach, and the advanced IRB approach for the calculation of credit risk capital under Basel II.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under the IRB approach for retail exposures, residential mortgages are assigned a higher asset correlation than qualifying revolving retail exposures.
cards.explanation: Residential mortgages are assigned a correlation of 0.15, against 0.04 for qualifying revolving retail exposures.
cards.originalText: Under the IRB approach for retail exposures, residential mortgages are assigned a higher asset correlation than qualifying revolving retail exposures

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Compare the standardized internal ratings-based (IRB) approach, the foundation IRB approach, and the advanced IRB approach for the calculation of credit risk capital under Basel II.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under the standardized approach, regulatory retail exposures are assigned a risk weight of 25%.
cards.explanation: The standardized risk weight for regulatory retail exposures is 75% (35% for residential mortgages).
cards.originalText: Under the standardized approach, ”regulatory retail” exposures are assigned a risk weight of 25%
cards.correction: Under the standardized approach, regulatory retail exposures are assigned a risk weight of 75%.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Compare the standardized internal ratings-based (IRB) approach, the foundation IRB approach, and the advanced IRB approach for the calculation of credit risk capital under Basel II.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Retail exposures must use the foundation IRB approach, with supervisory LGD and EAD.
cards.explanation: For retail exposures the foundation and advanced IRB approaches are merged, and the bank estimates PD, LGD and EAD itself, with no maturity adjustment.
cards.originalText: Retail exposures must use the foundation IRB approach, with supervisory LGD and EAD

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Calculate credit risk capital under Basel II utilizing the IRB approach.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: In Vasicek's model under Basel II, a higher correlation raises the capital requirement because defaults become more likely to occur together.
cards.explanation: Higher correlation means defaults cluster, fattening the tail of the loss distribution and raising the worst-case default rate and therefore capital.
cards.originalText: A higher $\rho$ raises capital because defaults become more likely to occur together.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Calculate credit risk capital under Basel II utilizing the IRB approach.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: In Vasicek's model under Basel II, a higher correlation lowers the capital requirement because defaults are more diversified across the portfolio.
cards.explanation: Higher correlation means less diversification. It raises the 99.9% worst-case default rate and therefore capital.
cards.originalText: A higher $\rho$ lowers capital because defaults are more diversified across the portfolio.
cards.correction: In Vasicek's model under Basel II, a higher correlation raises the capital requirement because defaults are more likely to occur together.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Calculate credit risk capital under Basel II utilizing the IRB approach.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: In Vasicek's model under Basel II, the confidence level determines the worst-case default rate that the bank must be able to withstand.
cards.explanation: The confidence level X picks the percentile of the default-rate distribution, so a 99.9% level gives a worst-case default rate that the bank is 99.9% sure will not be exceeded in a year.
cards.originalText: It determines the worst‑case default rate (WCDR) that the bank must be able to withstand.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Calculate credit risk capital under Basel II utilizing the IRB approach.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: In Vasicek's model under Basel II, the confidence level sets the threshold for the expected loss that capital must cover.
cards.explanation: Expected loss depends on PD and is covered by pricing and provisions. The confidence level determines the worst-case default rate, which drives the unexpected loss that capital covers.
cards.originalText: It sets the threshold for the expected loss that capital must cover.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Calculate credit risk capital under Basel II utilizing the IRB approach.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: In Vasicek's model under Basel II, the worst-case default rate depends only on PD, the asset correlation and the confidence level.
cards.explanation: WCDR = N[(N^-1(PD) + sqrt(rho) N^-1(X)) / sqrt(1 - rho)]. LGD, EAD and maturity enter only when WCDR is converted into capital.
cards.originalText: PD, the asset (copula) correlation and the confidence level

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Calculate credit risk capital under Basel II utilizing the IRB approach.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: In Vasicek's model under Basel II, the worst-case default rate formula requires PD, LGD, EAD and maturity as inputs.
cards.explanation: LGD, EAD and maturity are used later to convert the worst-case default rate into dollar capital. The WCDR formula itself needs only PD, the correlation and the confidence level.
cards.originalText: PD, LGD, EAD and maturity

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Calculate credit risk capital under Basel II utilizing the IRB approach.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under the Basel II IRB approach, credit risk capital is based on a value at risk calculation with a one-year horizon and 99.9% confidence.
cards.explanation: The IRB approach sets capital to cover credit losses over one year with 99.9% certainty. The capital required is this VaR minus expected loss.
cards.originalText: Value at risk with a one‑year horizon and 99.9% confidence.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Calculate credit risk capital under Basel II utilizing the IRB approach.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under the Basel II IRB approach, credit risk capital is based on a value at risk calculation with a one-year horizon and 99% confidence.
cards.explanation: The IRB confidence level is 99.9%, not 99%.
cards.originalText: Value at risk with a one‑year horizon and 99% confidence.
cards.correction: Under the Basel II IRB approach, credit risk capital is based on a value at risk calculation with a one-year horizon and 99.9% confidence.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Calculate credit risk capital under Basel II utilizing the IRB approach.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under the Basel II IRB approach, credit risk capital is based on a value at risk calculation with a 10-day horizon and 99% confidence.
cards.explanation: A 10-day, 99% VaR is the 1996 Amendment standard for market risk. IRB credit risk capital uses a one-year horizon and 99.9% confidence.
cards.originalText: Value at risk with a 10‑day horizon and 99% confidence.
cards.correction: Under the Basel II IRB approach, credit risk capital is based on a value at risk calculation with a one-year horizon and 99.9% confidence.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Calculate credit risk capital under Basel II utilizing the IRB approach.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: In the asymptotic single risk factor model underlying the Basel II IRB risk weights, the capital charge for an exposure depends only on the risk characteristics of that exposure itself.
cards.explanation: The ASRF model assumes a large, granular portfolio, so capital is portfolio-invariant: it does not depend on the composition of the portfolio to which the exposure is added.
cards.originalText: The capital charge depends only on the risk characteristics of the exposure itself.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Calculate credit risk capital under Basel II utilizing the IRB approach.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: In the asymptotic single risk factor model underlying the Basel II IRB risk weights, the capital charge for an exposure depends on the composition of the portfolio to which it is added.
cards.explanation: The ASRF model is portfolio-invariant: capital depends only on the exposure's own risk characteristics, and capital is additive across exposures.
cards.originalText: The capital charge depends on the composition of the portfolio to which the exposure is added.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Calculate credit risk capital under Basel II utilizing the IRB approach.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: In the asymptotic single risk factor model underlying the Basel II IRB risk weights, the capital charge for an exposure is independent of the exposure's PD.
cards.explanation: Capital rises with PD through the worst-case default rate and the (WCDR - PD) term, so it depends on PD.
cards.originalText: The capital charge is independent of the exposure’s PD.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the stressed VaR introduced in Basel 2.5 and calculate the market risk capital charge.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Moving from Basel II to Basel II.5 increases capital charges for market risk.
cards.explanation: Basel II.5 added stressed VaR, the incremental risk charge and the comprehensive risk measure to the trading book rules, all of which add to market risk capital.
cards.originalText: Capital charges for market risk will increase.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the stressed VaR introduced in Basel 2.5 and calculate the market risk capital charge.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Moving from Basel II to Basel II.5 brought sweeping changes in liquidity measurement techniques.
cards.explanation: Liquidity measures such as the LCR and NSFR came with Basel III, not Basel II.5.
cards.originalText: Sweeping changes in liquidity measurement techniques.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the stressed VaR introduced in Basel 2.5 and calculate the market risk capital charge.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The calculation of the net stable funding ratio and the liquidity coverage ratio was introduced through Basel 2.5.
cards.explanation: The liquidity ratios were introduced by Basel III. Basel 2.5 introduced stressed VaR, the incremental risk charge and the comprehensive risk measure.
cards.originalText: Calculation of the net stable funding ratio (NSFR) and the liquidity coverage ratio (LCR).
cards.correction: The calculation of the net stable funding ratio and the liquidity coverage ratio was introduced through Basel III.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the stressed VaR introduced in Basel 2.5 and calculate the market risk capital charge.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Basel 2.5 implemented a new incremental risk charge.
cards.explanation: The incremental risk charge is one of the three Basel 2.5 trading book changes, with stressed VaR and the comprehensive risk measure.
cards.originalText: Implementation of a new incremental risk charge (IRC).

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the stressed VaR introduced in Basel 2.5 and calculate the market risk capital charge.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Basel 2.5 introduced a comprehensive risk measure for instruments sensitive to correlations between default risks.
cards.explanation: The comprehensive risk measure for correlation-sensitive instruments is one of the three Basel 2.5 trading book changes, with stressed VaR and the incremental risk charge.
cards.originalText: A comprehensive risk measure (CRM) for instruments sensitive to correlations between default risks.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the stressed VaR introduced in Basel 2.5 and calculate the market risk capital charge.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Basel 2.5 expanded the VaR computation to include a stressed VaR component.
cards.explanation: Adding stressed VaR to the traditional VaR is the first of the three Basel 2.5 trading book changes, made because market risk capital had proved insufficient.
cards.originalText: VaR computation was expanded to include a stressed VaR component

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the stressed VaR introduced in Basel 2.5 and calculate the market risk capital charge.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Basel 2.5 introduced the requirement to hold operational risk capital on top of credit and market risk capital.
cards.explanation: Operational risk capital was introduced with Basel II in 2004. Basel 2.5 changed the trading book rules.
cards.originalText: A portion of operational risk capital was required on top of credit and market risk
cards.correction: Basel II introduced the requirement to hold operational risk capital on top of credit and market risk capital.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the stressed VaR introduced in Basel 2.5 and calculate the market risk capital charge.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Basel 2.5 designated Tier 1 capital for going-concern loss absorption and Tier 2 capital for recapitalising an institution in resolution.
cards.explanation: That description of the capital tiers belongs to Basel III. Basel 2.5 changed the trading book rules with stressed VaR, the incremental risk charge and the comprehensive risk measure.
cards.originalText: Tier 1 capital was designated for going‑concern loss absorption, while Tier 2 capital was to be used for recapitalizing an institution in resolution
cards.correction: Basel III designated Tier 1 capital for going-concern loss absorption and Tier 2 capital for recapitalising an institution in resolution.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the stressed VaR introduced in Basel 2.5 and calculate the market risk capital charge.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The main changes introduced by Basel II.5 are stressed VaR, a new incremental risk charge, and a comprehensive risk measure for instruments dependent on credit correlation.
cards.explanation: These are the three Basel II.5 trading book changes. Liquidity ratios and changes to IRB parameters are not part of Basel II.5.
cards.originalText: Stressed VaR, a new incremental risk charge, and a comprehensive risk measure for instruments dependent on credit correlation.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the stressed VaR introduced in Basel 2.5 and calculate the market risk capital charge.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Stressed VaR was introduced under Basel II.5 mainly because VaR had become too low as a result of low volatility of market variables.
cards.explanation: After prolonged calm periods, VaR based on recent data drifted down and was slow to respond when volatility rose in 2007. Stressed VaR uses a stressful period so the measure stays large.
cards.originalText: VaR that was too low as a result of low volatility of market variables.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the stressed VaR introduced in Basel 2.5 and calculate the market risk capital charge.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Stressed VaR was introduced under Basel II.5 mainly because of very high capital requirements caused by high volatility of market variables.
cards.explanation: The concern was the opposite: capital was too low, because VaR was low after a long period of low volatility.
cards.originalText: very high capital requirements caused by high volatility of market variables.
cards.correction: Stressed VaR was introduced under Basel II.5 mainly because of very low capital requirements caused by low volatility of market variables.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the stressed VaR introduced in Basel 2.5 and calculate the market risk capital charge.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Basel 2.5, a bank must identify the most stressful one-year (250-day) period within the most recent seven years to calculate stressed VaR.
cards.explanation: The stress period is chosen as the 250-day window in the last seven years that is most stressful for the bank's own portfolio, so it can differ across banks.
cards.originalText: Banks must identify the most stressful one‑year (250‑day) period from the most recent seven years.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the stressed VaR introduced in Basel 2.5 and calculate the market risk capital charge.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Basel 2.5, a bank must use the most recent one-year period of historical data to calculate stressed VaR.
cards.explanation: The most recent year is typically calm. The stress period is the most stressful 250-day period within the last seven years for the bank's own portfolio.
cards.originalText: Banks must use the most recent one‑year period of historical data to calculate stressed VaR.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the stressed VaR introduced in Basel 2.5 and calculate the market risk capital charge.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Basel 2.5, all banks must use a fixed one-year period from the 2007-2008 financial crisis to calculate stressed VaR.
cards.explanation: A fixed common period such as 2008 was considered early on but dropped. Each bank identifies its own most stressful 250-day period in the last seven years.
cards.originalText: Banks must use a fixed one‑year period from the 2007‑2008 financial crisis for all portfolios.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the stressed VaR introduced in Basel 2.5 and calculate the market risk capital charge.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Market risk capital under Basel 2.5 should be close to double that under Basel II, due to the addition of the stressed VaR.
cards.explanation: Stressed VaR is added to, not substituted for, the normal VaR and is at least as large, so the market risk charge is roughly twice as large or more.
cards.originalText: Market risk capital under Basel 2.5 should be close to double that of market risk capital under Basel II due to the addition of the stressed VaR.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the stressed VaR introduced in Basel 2.5 and calculate the market risk capital charge.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Basel 2.5 established the year 2008 as the stress period, and all banks use data from 2008 to calculate stressed VaR.
cards.explanation: Each bank chooses its own most stressful 250-day period within the last seven years. A fixed 2008 period was only an early idea.
cards.originalText: Basel 2.5 has established the year 2008 as the ”stress” period. All banks use data from 2008 to calculate the stressed VaR.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the stressed VaR introduced in Basel 2.5 and calculate the market risk capital charge.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Stressed VaR under Basel 2.5 must be calculated using a 99.9% confidence level.
cards.explanation: Both the normal and the stressed VaR use a 10-day horizon and 99% confidence. The 99.9% level is the IRB credit risk standard.
cards.originalText: The stressed VaR must be calculated using a 99.9% confidence interval.
cards.correction: Stressed VaR under Basel 2.5 must be calculated using a 99% confidence level.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe and calculate ratios intended to improve the management of liquidity risk, including the required leverage ratio, the liquidity coverage ratio, and the net stable funding ratio.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Basel III, the liquidity coverage ratio is the ratio between high-quality liquid assets and net cash outflows over a 30-day period.
cards.explanation: The LCR compares the stock of high-quality liquid assets with stressed 30-day net cash outflows and must be at least 100%.
cards.originalText: Ratio between high‑quality liquid assets and net cash outflows in a 30‑day period.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe and calculate ratios intended to improve the management of liquidity risk, including the required leverage ratio, the liquidity coverage ratio, and the net stable funding ratio.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Basel III, the liquidity coverage ratio is the ratio between high-quality liquid assets and total assets.
cards.explanation: The LCR denominator is net cash outflows over a 30-day stress period, not total assets.
cards.originalText: Ratio between high‑quality liquid assets and total assets.
cards.correction: Under Basel III, the liquidity coverage ratio is the ratio between high-quality liquid assets and net cash outflows in a 30-day period.

changes.to: net cash outflows in a 30-day period

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe and calculate ratios intended to improve the management of liquidity risk, including the required leverage ratio, the liquidity coverage ratio, and the net stable funding ratio.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The liquidity coverage ratio focuses on a 30-day period, whereas the net stable funding ratio focuses on a 1-year period.
cards.explanation: The LCR is a short-term measure of the ability to withstand 30 days of disrupted liquidity. The NSFR is a longer-term structural measure over one year.
cards.originalText: LCR: Focuses on a 30‑day period; NSFR: Focuses on a 1‑year period.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe and calculate ratios intended to improve the management of liquidity risk, including the required leverage ratio, the liquidity coverage ratio, and the net stable funding ratio.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The liquidity coverage ratio focuses on a 30-day period, whereas the net stable funding ratio focuses on a 2-year period.
cards.explanation: The NSFR horizon is one year. A 2-year period appears nowhere in Basel III.
cards.originalText: LCR: Focuses on a 30‑day period; NSFR: Focuses on a 2‑year period.
cards.correction: The liquidity coverage ratio focuses on a 30-day period, whereas the net stable funding ratio focuses on a 1-year period.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe and calculate ratios intended to improve the management of liquidity risk, including the required leverage ratio, the liquidity coverage ratio, and the net stable funding ratio.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The denominator of the Basel III leverage ratio is balance sheet assets without risk weighting, plus some off-balance-sheet items such as loan commitments.
cards.explanation: The leverage ratio is a non-risk-based backstop equal to capital divided by total exposure, with a 3% minimum. The other capital ratios divide by risk-weighted assets.
cards.originalText: The denominator of the leverage ratio is assets on the balance sheet without risk weighting (plus some off‑balance‑sheet items such as loan commitments)

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe and calculate ratios intended to improve the management of liquidity risk, including the required leverage ratio, the liquidity coverage ratio, and the net stable funding ratio.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The Basel III leverage ratio is defined in terms of cash inflows and cash outflows, and so provides an additional buffer against liquidity risk.
cards.explanation: Cash inflows and outflows describe the LCR. The leverage ratio is capital divided by unweighted total exposure.
cards.originalText: The leverage ratio is defined in terms of cash inflows and cash outflows and therefore provides an additional buffer against liquidity risk

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe and calculate ratios intended to improve the management of liquidity risk, including the required leverage ratio, the liquidity coverage ratio, and the net stable funding ratio.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The numerator of the Basel III leverage ratio is not regulatory capital but is adjusted for the risk of the funding source.
cards.explanation: The numerator is still regulatory capital. Adjusting funding for its risk describes the available stable funding factors in the NSFR.
cards.originalText: The numerator of the leverage ratio is not regulatory capital; rather, it is adjusted for the risk of the funding source

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe and calculate ratios intended to improve the management of liquidity risk, including the required leverage ratio, the liquidity coverage ratio, and the net stable funding ratio.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The net stable funding ratio will increase if retail deposits are replaced by wholesale deposits and marketable securities are replaced by residential mortgages.
cards.explanation: Wholesale deposits have lower stable funding factors than retail deposits, and mortgages require more stable funding than marketable securities, so available funding falls, required funding rises and the NSFR decreases.
cards.originalText: The NSFR will increase if retail deposits are replaced by wholesale deposits and marketable securities are replaced by residential mortgages.
cards.correction: The net stable funding ratio will decrease if retail deposits are replaced by wholesale deposits and marketable securities are replaced by residential mortgages.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe and calculate ratios intended to improve the management of liquidity risk, including the required leverage ratio, the liquidity coverage ratio, and the net stable funding ratio.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The net stable funding ratio is the ratio of weighted stable funding sources (liabilities and equity) to weighted assets requiring stable funding.
cards.explanation: NSFR = available stable funding (liability and equity side) divided by required stable funding (asset side).
cards.originalText: The NSFR is the ratio of weighted stable funding sources (liabilities and equity) to weighted assets requiring stable funding.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe and calculate ratios intended to improve the management of liquidity risk, including the required leverage ratio, the liquidity coverage ratio, and the net stable funding ratio.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The Basel III leverage ratio is capital divided by total exposure, which includes unweighted balance sheet items and some off-balance-sheet items, with a 3% minimum.
cards.explanation: The leverage ratio is a non-risk-based backstop: exposures are not risk weighted and the minimum is 3%.
cards.originalText: The Basel III leverage ratio is capital divided by total exposure, which includes unweighted balance sheet items and some off‑balance‑sheet items, with a 3% minimum.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe and calculate ratios intended to improve the management of liquidity risk, including the required leverage ratio, the liquidity coverage ratio, and the net stable funding ratio.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Basel III, only the net stable funding ratio counts the bank's Tier 1 and Tier 2 capital as a funding source in its numerator, with a 100% weighting factor.
cards.explanation: The NSFR numerator is available stable funding, built from the liability and equity side of the balance sheet, and Tier 1 and Tier 2 capital receive a 100% ASF factor. The LCR numerator is a stock of high-quality liquid assets, so capital never enters it.
cards.originalText: The net stable funding ratio only

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe and calculate ratios intended to improve the management of liquidity risk, including the required leverage ratio, the liquidity coverage ratio, and the net stable funding ratio.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Basel III, the liquidity coverage ratio numerator counts the bank's Tier 1 and Tier 2 capital as a funding source with a 100% weighting factor.
cards.explanation: The LCR numerator is a stock of high-quality liquid assets, not a funding measure. Capital is counted at a 100% ASF factor in the numerator of the net stable funding ratio.
cards.originalText: The liquidity coverage ratio only
cards.correction: Under Basel III, the net stable funding ratio numerator counts the bank's Tier 1 and Tier 2 capital as a funding source with a 100% weighting factor.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe and calculate ratios intended to improve the management of liquidity risk, including the required leverage ratio, the liquidity coverage ratio, and the net stable funding ratio.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Replacing zero-risk-weight government bonds with corporate loans, with funding unchanged, lowers the LCR, because the bonds count as HQLA without a haircut whereas loans do not count as HQLA.
cards.explanation: The swap removes HQLA from the LCR numerator while net 30-day cash outflows stay the same, so the ratio falls.
cards.originalText: The LCR will decrease because government bonds count as HQLA without a haircut, whereas corporate loans do not count as HQLA.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe and calculate ratios intended to improve the management of liquidity risk, including the required leverage ratio, the liquidity coverage ratio, and the net stable funding ratio.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Replacing zero-risk-weight government bonds with corporate loans improves the NSFR, because loans are short-term assets that need little stable funding.
cards.explanation: Loans carry higher required stable funding factors than zero-risk-weight government bonds, so the swap worsens the NSFR.
cards.originalText: The NSFR will improve because loans are short‑term assets that need little stable funding.
cards.correction: Replacing zero-risk-weight government bonds with corporate loans worsens the NSFR, because loans need more stable funding than government bonds.

changes.from: loans are short-term assets that need little stable funding
changes.to: loans need more stable funding than government bonds

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe and calculate ratios intended to improve the management of liquidity risk, including the required leverage ratio, the liquidity coverage ratio, and the net stable funding ratio.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Replacing zero-risk-weight government bonds with higher-yielding corporate loans increases the LCR, because loans earn a higher return than government bonds.
cards.explanation: The LCR depends on the quality of liquid assets, not on their return. Loans are not HQLA, so the swap reduces the LCR numerator.
cards.originalText: The LCR will increase because loans earn a higher return than government bonds.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.loText: Summarize the December 2017 revisions to the Basel III framework in the following areas: - The standardized approach to credit risk - The internal ratings-based (IRB) approaches for credit risk - The CVA risk framework - The operational risk framework - The leverage ratio framework
cards.reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.statement: Under the December 2017 revisions to the CVA risk framework, the internal model approach was removed and banks must use either the standardized approach (SA-CVA) or the basic approach (BA-CVA).
cards.explanation: To improve robustness and comparability, the internal model option for CVA risk was eliminated, leaving SA-CVA and the simpler BA-CVA.
cards.originalText: The internal model approach was removed; banks must use the standardized approach (SA‑CVA) or the basic approach (BA‑CVA).

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.loText: Summarize the December 2017 revisions to the Basel III framework in the following areas: - The standardized approach to credit risk - The internal ratings-based (IRB) approaches for credit risk - The CVA risk framework - The operational risk framework - The leverage ratio framework
cards.reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.statement: Under the December 2017 revisions to the CVA risk framework, the internal model approach was retained as the primary method, with the standardized approach as a fallback.
cards.explanation: The reform reversed this: the internal model approach for CVA risk was removed, and banks use SA-CVA or BA-CVA.
cards.originalText: The internal model approach was retained as the primary method, with the standardized approach as a fallback.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.loText: Summarize the December 2017 revisions to the Basel III framework in the following areas: - The standardized approach to credit risk - The internal ratings-based (IRB) approaches for credit risk - The CVA risk framework - The operational risk framework - The leverage ratio framework
cards.reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.statement: Under the December 2017 revisions to the CVA risk framework, all banks must use a single basic approach (BA-CVA) regardless of size or sophistication.
cards.explanation: Two approaches remain, the standardized approach (SA-CVA) and the basic approach (BA-CVA), so banks are not all confined to BA-CVA.
cards.originalText: All banks must use a single basic approach (BA‑CVA) regardless of size or sophistication.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.loText: Summarize the December 2017 revisions to the Basel III framework in the following areas: - The standardized approach to credit risk - The internal ratings-based (IRB) approaches for credit risk - The CVA risk framework - The operational risk framework - The leverage ratio framework
cards.reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.statement: Under the December 2017 revisions, CVA risk is no longer capitalized separately because it is already covered by the market risk framework.
cards.explanation: CVA risk remains a separately capitalized risk. The revisions made the CVA framework consistent with the revised market risk framework rather than merging it into it.
cards.originalText: CVA risk is no longer capitalized because it is already covered by the market risk framework.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.loText: Summarize the December 2017 revisions to the Basel III framework in the following areas: - The standardized approach to credit risk - The internal ratings-based (IRB) approaches for credit risk - The CVA risk framework - The operational risk framework - The leverage ratio framework
cards.reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.statement: The new standardized approach for operational risk capital assumes that banks with greater historical operational risk losses are more likely to experience operational risk losses in the future.
cards.explanation: Historical losses are one of the two inputs of the new standardized approach, alongside income, and they are assumed to be positively related to future operational risk losses.
cards.originalText: II only

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.loText: Summarize the December 2017 revisions to the Basel III framework in the following areas: - The standardized approach to credit risk - The internal ratings-based (IRB) approaches for credit risk - The CVA risk framework - The operational risk framework - The leverage ratio framework
cards.reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.statement: The new standardized approach for operational risk capital assumes that operational risk increases at a decreasing rate with a bank's income.
cards.explanation: The approach assumes operational risk rises at an increasing rate as income grows, which is why the marginal capital rates rise with the size bucket.
cards.originalText: I only
cards.correction: The new standardized approach for operational risk capital assumes that operational risk increases at an increasing rate with a bank's income.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
